text: Generative AI for game development, advanced applications in C# and Unity. Build the Emberlight Tavern, Unity, C#, and AI-driven NPCs in one modular scene. Hello, this is Liam in for Bear. Unity plus AI sounds like rewriting your whole dialogue system. It isn't. Modular scripts and JSON trees, the AI plugs in through one flag. Six terms, then we're off. Dialogue tree, nodes of lines and choices. NPC controller binds a character to its JSON. Dialogue manager loads and runs the trees. Emotion engine reads tone from keywords. AI response handler prompts the model, returns text. Mood meter, the UI showing inferred tone. The Emberlight Tavern, a candlelit medieval room with three souls in it.

The bartender, stoic and factual. The rogue, sarcastic and evasive. The minstrel, empathic and reactive. Plus a mood meter reading the tone of your every choice. The project is modular from the start. Four C# scripts, JSON dialogue files, and prefabs, each with one job. Seven setup steps, scene, player, tavern, UI, NPC, dialogue system, compressed into one motion. Build it, wire it, press play. The pipeline exactly as the chapter draws it. The NPC controller hands off to the dialogue manager, which reads a node. AI nodes go to the response handler. Everything passes the emotion engine, and the Unity UI shows it all. JSON is the source of truth. Each node

Holds a speaker, a line, choices, and a use AI flag. A new NPC is a new JSON file, no code changes. The use AI flag is the whole trick. Scripted nodes play exactly as written. AI nodes generate. Mix them, the chapter says, and players can't tell where the writing ends. The dialogue manager orchestrates. It loads the trees from JSON, displays each node, spawns the choice buttons, and hooks every line into the emotion engine. The emotion engine reads tone from keywords, angry, sad, happy, fearful, neutral, and colors the mood meter. The chapter's exact logic run live. The AI response handler builds the prompt and calls a local model, llama, running on

Your own machine, capped at about 35 tokens. One short sentence. No cloud, no bill. And the NPC controller binds it all, a name and a dialogue file. Bartender plus bartender JSON, the character and their words linked. Press E, the rogue greets you with a static line, "Well, well, someone brave or foolish. Which are you?" Two choices appear beneath. Choose confrontation and you hit a use AI node. The handler builds the prompt, sarcastic rogue, dry wit, misdirection, and the AI fires back. Then why start with a riddle? "I have secrets you'd kill to know." The tone shifts from hostile to curious, and a second AI reply lands in character in

The moment. No two players hear the same tavern. Prefabs make it reusable. Choice buttons, the mood meter, the interact prompt built once, stamped everywhere. And the meter colors with the mood. Red for anger, blue for sorrow, green for joy. The honest limit keyword lists are brittle. Hostile reads neutral, kill reads neutral. Extend the lists, the chapter says, or graduate to real sentiment analysis. Generative AI, emotional analysis, modular architecture, one tavern, three souls, and a narrative system that feels alive. Let's recap with Claude, the Emberlight tavern, three NPCs, one mood meter, and a modular Unity scene. Six boxes form the pipeline, JSON trees are the source

Of truth. AI plugs in through one flag. Four C# scripts split the work, dialogue, emotion, AI, and character binding. The rogue walk-through proves it. Static greetings, AI wit, shifting tone. Prefabs keep it reusable. The keyword engine's limits keep it honest. Generative AI plus modular architecture, narrative systems that feel alive. Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Help me design one NPC for a Unity dialogue system like the Emberlight tavern. I will describe the character. You write a JSON dialogue node with speaker text and two player choices. One choice leading to a scripted node, one to use AI node. Write the prompt the AI response handler would send for the AI node and list SIX

Mood keywords covering at least two emotions for the emotion engine. Then test me, give me a player line and ask what mood the keyword engine detects. Then check two things yourself. Does the AI prompt constrain the character's voice, not just the topic? And would your keyword list actually catch the words your players type? If hostile reads as neutral, extend the lists before you ship. Advanced applications in C# and Unity at Nick Bear Brown.
